back: Systemic release of IL-6 triggers the liver to produce acute-phase proteins (e.g., CRP), contributing to anemia and fatigue.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1086 (Book Page): [Systemic release of IL-6 triggers production of acute phase proteins by the liver.]

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Define the clinical triad and hematological associations found in Felty Syndrome.
back: Triad: Rheumatoid Arthritis, Splenomegaly, and Neutropenia. Often associated with thrombocytopenia and high-titer Rheumatoid Factor.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1089 (Book Page): [Felty syndrome is a rare complication of seropositive RA in which splenomegaly occurs in combination with neutropenia and thrombocytopenia.]

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: How does angiogenesis contribute to the persistence of synovitis in RA?
back: New blood vessels express activated endothelial cells that recruit more leucocytes into the synovium, perpetuating the inflammatory process.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1086 (Book Page): [Within these blood vessels, pro-inflammatory cytokines activate endothelial cells, which support recruitment of yet more leucocytes to perpetuate the inflammatory process.]

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What are the characteristic histological findings within a Rheumatoid Nodule?
back: A central area of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by a palisade of proliferating mononuclear cells (macrophages and fibroblasts).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1086 (Book Page): [They consist of a central area of fibrinoid material surrounded by a palisade of proliferating mononuclear cells.]

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What is the strongest genetic association with Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) susceptibility?
back: The HLA-DRB1 'shared epitope' is the strongest link, specifically determined by amino acid variations at positions 11, 71, and 74.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1087 (Book Page): The strongest association is with variants in the HLA region and is determined by variations in three amino acids in the HLA-DRβ1 molecule (positions 11, 71 and 74).

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: How does citrullination contribute to RA immunopathogenesis?
back: Environmental stimuli (e.g., smoking) trigger post-translational modification of host proteins (citrullination), rendering them immunogenic and inducing autoantibody production (ACPA).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1087 (Book Page): RA occurs when an environmental stimulus... triggers autoimmunity... by modifying host proteins, through processes like citrullination, so that they become immunogenic.

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Compare the diagnostic specificity of ACPA versus Rheumatoid Factor (RF) in RA.
back: Anti-Citrullinated Peptide Antibodies (ACPA) are highly specific for RA, whereas RF is less specific and occurs in other conditions.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1090 (Book Page): Tests for ACPA are positive in about 70% of cases and are highly specific for RA... RF is less specific than ACPA, however, and positive tests can occur in other diseases.

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: A patient with long-standing RA presents with new-onset occipital headache and arm paresthesia. Diagnosis?
back: Atlanto-axial subluxation. It results from erosion of the transverse ligament posterior to the odontoid peg by inflamed synovium.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1090 (Book Page): Atlanto-axial subluxation is due to erosion of the transverse ligament posterior to the odontoid peg... suspected in any RA patient who describes new onset of occipital headache, particularly if... paraesthesia... are present in the arms.

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Explain the role of TNF-α in the RA synovial inflammatory loop.
back: TNF-α (from macrophages/T-cells) activates synovial fibroblasts to produce more cytokines and Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs), perpetuating tissue degradation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1087 (Book Page): Macrophages produce... TNF-α, IL-1 and IL-6, which act on synovial fibroblasts to produce further cytokines, setting up a positive feedback loop.

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What is the threshold score for 'definite RA' under 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria?
back: A total score of ≥ 6 out of 10 is required.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1088 (Book Page): Patients with a score ≥ 6 are considered to have definite RA.

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What specific mechanism drives bone erosions at the joint margin in RA?
back: Osteoclast activation stimulated by RANKL (from activated T cells) and M-CSF (from synovial cells) within the pannus.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1087 (Book Page): A key pathogenic factor in bone erosions... is osteoclast activation, stimulated by the production of M-CSF by synovial cells and RANKL by activated T cells.

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: How does Felty syndrome differ from typical RA presentation?
back: It presents as a triad of long-standing seropositive RA, splenomegaly, and neutropenia (increasing infection risk).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1090 (Book Page): Felty syndrome is a rare complication... in which splenomegaly occurs in combination with neutropenia and thrombocytopenia.

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Explain the link between systemic IL-6 release and lab findings in active RA.
back: IL-6 triggers hepatic production of acute-phase proteins, resulting in elevated CRP and ESR levels.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1087 (Book Page): Systemic release of IL-6 triggers production of acute phase proteins by the liver.

category: Explain the immunopathogenesis and underlying mechanisms leading to Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Define 'pannus' and its pathological role in Rheumatoid Arthritis.
back: Pannus is hypertrophied, highly vascular, inflamed synovium that directly invades and destroys cartilage and bone.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1087 (Book Page): The inflamed synovium (pannus) directly invades bone and cartilage to cause joint erosions... New blood-vessel formation (angiogenesis) occurs, causing the inflamed synovium to become highly vascular.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: List the primary modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors for the development of Osteoarthritis (OA).
back: Modifiable: Obesity, repetitive joint loading (occupational), and joint trauma. Non-modifiable: Advancing age, female gender, and genetic predisposition.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Box 26.36 Risk factors for osteoarthritis: Genetics, Developmental abnormalities, Repetitive loading, Adverse biomechanics, Obesity, Trauma, Hormonal]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Which specific occupations are classically associated with an increased risk of Osteoarthritis at particular joints?
back: Farmers (Hip OA), Miners (Knee OA), and Elite or professional athletes (Knee and ankle OA).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Biomechanical factors play an important role in OA related to certain occupations, such as farmers (hip OA), miners (knee OA) and elite or professional athletes (knee and ankle OA).]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: How do developmental structural abnormalities like Slipped Femoral Epiphysis contribute to early-onset hip Osteoarthritis?
back: These conditions cause abnormal load distribution across the joint, leading to premature articular cartilage degeneration and subchondral bone changes.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Structural abnormalities, such as slipped femoral epiphysis and developmental dysplasia of the hip, are also associated with a high risk of OA, presumably due to abnormal load distribution across the joint.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: A post-menopausal woman on Aromatase Inhibitors for breast cancer develops joint pain. Identify the hormonal risk factor.
back: Estrogen deficiency (post-menopause) and Aromatase Inhibitor therapy are significant hormonal factors that contribute to the development and progression of OA.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Oestrogen appears important; lower rates of OA have been observed in women who use hormone replacement therapy (HRT), while women who receive aromatase inhibitor therapy for breast cancer often experience a flare in symptoms of OA.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Beyond mechanical stress, how does obesity contribute to the systemic progression of Osteoarthritis?
back: Adipose tissue releases pro-inflammatory cytokines (adipokines) that facilitate cartilage matrix degradation and metabolic-driven joint inflammation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [There is a strong association between obesity and OA... it has also been speculated that cytokines released from adipose tissue may play a role.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: What is the estimated genetic heritability of Osteoarthritis in the hip and hand joints?
back: Hip heritability is 60%, while hand joints are 65%. Most cases are polygenic, mediated by several variants of small effect.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Family-based studies have estimated that the heritability of OA ranges from about 43% at the knee to between 60% and 65% at the hip and hand, respectively.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Why does a history of meniscectomy or cruciate ligament rupture significantly increase knee OA risk?
back: These injuries act as 'destabilising injuries' that alter joint biomechanics, concentrating mechanical stress on articular cartilage, leading to focal loss.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [There is also a high risk of knee OA in people who have had destabilising injuries, such as cruciate ligament rupture, and those who have had meniscectomy.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Which metabolic and endocrine disorders are high-yield risk factors for atypical or early-onset Osteoarthritis?
back: Haemochromatosis, Ochronosis, Acromegaly, and Alkaptonuria are classic systemic conditions that predispose to premature joint degeneration.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1076 (Book Page): [Box 26.39 Causes of early-onset osteoarthritis: Metabolic or endocrine disease: Haemochromatosis, Ochronosis, Acromegaly, Alkaptonuria]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Identify the cultural/biomechanical factor hypothesized to contribute to higher knee OA prevalence in South and East Asia.
back: Frequent and prolonged squatting is speculated to be a key biomechanical risk factor for the higher prevalence of knee OA in these regions.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [It has been speculated that the higher prevalence of knee OA in South and East Asia might be accounted for by squatting.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: How does Osteoarthritis risk relate to age and which gender faces a higher lifetime risk of joint replacement?
back: Risk rises progressively with age. Women have a higher lifetime risk (11% for knee/hip) compared to men (8%).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [The prevalence rises progressively with age... the lifetime risk of having a total hip or knee replacement for OA in someone aged 50 is about 11% for women and 8% for men in the UK.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: How does age primarily influence the epidemiology of Osteoarthritis (OA)?
back: The prevalence of OA rises progressively with age, making it a major cause of disability in the elderly.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [The prevalence rises progressively with age and it has been estimated that 45% of all people develop knee OA and 25% hip OA at some point during life.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
coreConcept: Metabolic and Biomechanical Risks of Obesity
front: Q: Which two mechanisms link obesity to the progression of knee Osteoarthritis?
back: 1. Biomechanical load distribution. 2. Pro-inflammatory cytokines released from adipose tissue.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [This is thought to be due partly to biomechanical factors, but it has also been speculated that cytokines released from adipose tissue may play a role.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Identify the specific high-risk occupations for hip and knee Osteoarthritis.
back: 1. Farmers (Hip OA). 2. Miners and elite athletes (Knee OA).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [certain occupations, such as farmers (hip OA), miners (knee OA) and elite or professional athletes (knee and ankle OA).]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Which two developmental hip abnormalities are major risk factors for secondary OA?
back: 1. Slipped femoral epiphysis. 2. Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Structural abnormalities, such as slipped femoral epiphysis and developmental dysplasia of the hip, are also associated with a high risk of OA, presumably due to abnormal load distribution.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Which specific traumatic knee injuries lead to a high risk of subsequent OA?
back: 1. Cruciate ligament rupture. 2. Meniscectomy.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [high risk of knee OA in people who have had destabilising injuries, such as cruciate ligament rupture, and those who have had meniscectomy.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: How do hormonal factors and specific cancer therapies influence OA symptoms in women?
back: Estrogen deficiency increases risk (HRT is protective), while aromatase inhibitors flare OA symptoms.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Oestr ogen appears important; lower rates of OA have been observed in women who use hormone replacement therapy (HRT), while women who receive aromatase inhibitor therapy for breast cancer often experience a flare.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Contrast the genetic heritability of OA between the knee and hip joints.
back: Knee heritability is approximately 43%, whereas hip heritability is higher at 60-65%.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [heritability of OA ranges from about 43% at the knee to between 60% and 65% at the hip and hand, respectively.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: List four metabolic or endocrine triggers for early-onset polyarticular Osteoarthritis.
back: 1. Haemochromatosis. 2. Ochronosis (Alkaptonuria). 3. Acromegaly. 4. Wilson’s disease.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1076 (Book Page): [Box 26.39: Metabolic or endocrine disease: Haemochromatosis, Ochronosis, Acromegaly, Alkaptonuria.] Page 1081 (Book Page): [Box 26.45: Wilson’s disease.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: What unique cultural biomechanical factor is associated with knee OA in South Asia?
back: Prolonged squatting is speculated to contribute to the higher prevalence of knee OA in the region.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [speculated that the higher prevalence of knee OA in South and East Asia might be accounted for by squatting.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: How does systemic Bone Mineral Density (BMD) relate to Osteoarthritis risk?
back: High BMD is associated with increased OA risk (osteophyte formation) and protects against osteoporosis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1074 (Book Page): [patients with OA have higher BMD values at sites distant from the joint... associated with osteophyte formation. This is in keeping with... patients with OA are partially protected from developing osteoporosis.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: What is the recommended first-line oral analgesic for Osteoarthritis (OA) management when non-pharmacological measures fail?
back: Paracetamol is the initial trial; if insufficient, topical NSAIDs or capsaicin (for knee/hand) followed by oral NSAIDs should be considered.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1077 (Book Page): If symptoms do not respond to non-pharmacological measures, paracetamol should be tried. Addition of a topical NSAID and then capsaicin for knee and hand OA can also be helpful.

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: Outline the typical pharmacological management plan for a newly diagnosed Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) patient.
back: 1. Prompt cDMARD initiation (e.g., Methotrexate weekly). 2. Glucocorticoid bridge (e.g., Prednisolone 30mg daily, tapered over 12 weeks). 3. Folic acid supplementation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1090 (Book Page): Prompt initiation of cDMARD therapy is indicated... prednisolone can be started in a dose of 30 mg daily gradually reducing... methotrexate (MTX) should be started in an initial dose of 15 mg weekly, along with folic acid.

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: When is total joint replacement surgery indicated in the management plan for Osteoarthritis?
back: Indicated for severe disabling hip or knee OA where symptoms and functional impairment impact quality of life despite optimal medical and lifestyle therapy.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1077 (Book Page): Surgery should be considered for patients with OA whose symptoms and functional impairment impact significantly on their quality of life despite optimal medical therapy and lifestyle advice.

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: Management Plan: What drug adjustments must be made for an RA patient planning to conceive?
back: 1. Stop Methotrexate (MTX) ≥3 months prior. 2. Stop Leflunomide ≥24 months prior. 3. Switch to safe DMARDs like Sulfasalazine or Hydroxychloroquine.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1091 (Book Page): methotrexate should be discontinued for ≥ 3 months and leflunomide discontinued for ≥ 24 months before trying to conceive... DMARDs that may be used: sulfasalazine, azathioprine and hydroxychloroquine.

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: How should transient disease flares be managed in a patient already established on DMARD/Biologic therapy?
back: 1. Local intra-articular glucocorticoid injections. 2. Deep intramuscular 'depot' steroid injections. 3. Short course of oral Prednisolone.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1091 (Book Page): Transient flares can be dealt with by local joint or deep IM ‘depot’ steroid injections or a short course of oral prednisolone.

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: What are the first-line non-pharmacological management steps for lower limb Osteoarthritis?
back:
• Weight loss (if obese)
• Strengthening and aerobic exercises (specifically quadriceps exercises for knee OA)
• Shock-absorbing footwear and walking sticks
• Education on the condition and pacing activities.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1077 (Book Page): [Weight loss has a substantial beneficial effect... Strengthening and aerobic exercises also have beneficial effects... Quadriceps strengthening exercises are particularly beneficial in knee OA.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: Outline the pharmacological 'step-up' plan for Rheumatoid Arthritis patients failing initial Methotrexate monotherapy.
back:
• Step 2: Triple therapy (Methotrexate + Sulfasalazine + Hydroxychloroquine)
• Step 3: Substitute subcutaneous MTX or change cDMARDs
• Step 4: Add biological therapy (usually anti-TNF-α) or tsDMARD if DAS28 remains ≥ 3.2.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1091 (Book Page): [Algorithm for the management of rheumatoid arthritis: MTX 15 mg weekly... Add SSZ and HCQ... Add biologic or tsDMARD if DAS28 ≥ 3.2.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: What is the management goal and titration protocol for Allopurinol in chronic Gout?
back:
• Target: Serum Urate < 300 μmol/L (5 mg/dL).
• Protocol: Start 100 mg daily (50 mg in elderly/renal impairment); increase by 100 mg every 4 weeks until target reached.
• Prophylaxis: Co-prescribe low-dose Colchicine or NSAIDs for the first few months.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1081 (Book Page): [The recommended starting dose is 100 mg daily... increased by 100 mg every 4 weeks... until the target uric acid level is achieved... therapeutic target of < 300 μmol/L.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: Outline the emergency management plan for suspected Septic Arthritis before culture results are available.
back:
• Urgent joint aspiration (Gram stain/culture) and blood cultures.
• Admit for IV antibiotics: Flucloxacillin (2g QDS) first-line.
• Penicillin-allergic: IV Vancomycin or Clindamycin.
• Daily needle aspiration to dryness and early passive movement.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1084 (Book Page): [Emergency management of suspected septic arthritis: Aspirate joint... Flucloxacillin (2 g four times daily)... Perform serial needle aspiration to dryness.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: What is the standard management plan for organ-threatening or severe Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)?
back:
• High-dose glucocorticoids (e.g., pulsed IV Methylprednisolone).
• Immunosuppressants: Cyclophosphamide (IV pulses every 2–3 weeks) or Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF).
• Maintenance: Azathioprine or MMF with lowest effective steroid dose.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1100 (Book Page): [High-dose glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants are required... pulsed methylprednisolone (10 mg/kg IV) plus cyclophosphamide (15 mg/kg IV).]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: What is the immediate management plan for Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) to prevent permanent visual loss?
back:
• High-dose Prednisolone (40–60 mg daily) initiated immediately on clinical suspicion.
• Urgent Ophthalmology referral if visual symptoms exist.
• Add Tocilizumab in high-risk patients to reduce steroid dependence.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1106 (Book Page): [Prednisolone should be commenced urgently in suspected GCA... 40–60 mg... tocilizumab has been shown to reduce the risk of relapse.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: Outline the management adjustments for a Rheumatoid Arthritis patient planning conception.
back:
• Discontinue Methotrexate ≥ 3 months before conception.
• Discontinue Leflunomide ≥ 24 months before conception.
• Safe options: Sulfasalazine, Hydroxychloroquine, and Certolizumab (biologic of choice as it doesn't cross the placenta).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1091 (Book Page): [Conception: methotrexate should be discontinued for ≥ 3 months and leflunomide discontinued for ≥ 24 months... certolizumab, which does not cross the placenta.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: What is the life-saving management step for a Systemic Sclerosis (SScl) patient in a hypertensive renal crisis?
back:
• Aggressive treatment with ACE inhibitors (e.g., Captopril/Enalapril).
• Mandatory even if renal impairment is present; they reverse the vasoconstriction driving the crisis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1102 (Book Page): [Hypertensive renal crisis: Aggressive treatment with ACE inhibitors is needed, even if renal impairment is present.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: Outline the management plan for an acute flare of Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition (CPPD/Pseudogout).
back:
• Symptomatic: Ice packs, joint elevation, and aspiration for pain relief.
• Pharmacological: Intra-articular glucocorticoid injection (once infection is excluded).
• Oral: NSAIDs or low-dose Colchicine (0.5–2 mg daily).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1082 (Book Page): [In acute CPP crystal arthritis... joint aspiration provides symptomatic relief. Once infection is excluded, intra-articular glucocorticoid can be injected. NSAIDs and colchicine... are helpful.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: What is the surgical management plan for an Osteoarthritis patient whose quality of life is severely impacted despite medical therapy?
back:
• Total Joint Replacement (Arthroplasty) is the gold standard for severe hip/knee OA.
• Consideration: Refer before functional limitation is advanced to ensure better postoperative outcomes.
• Alternatives: Osteotomy (for younger patients with knee OA) or femoral head resurfacing.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1077 (Book Page): [Total joint replacement surgery is by far the most common... indicated when there is significant structural damage on X-ray... consider it before functional limitation has become advanced.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: What is the most effective non-pharmacological lifestyle intervention for symptom relief in lower limb osteoarthritis (OA)?
back: Weight loss (substantial effect on symptoms and progression) and quadriceps strengthening exercises.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1077 (Book Page): Weight loss has a substantial beneficial effect on symptoms if the patient is obese and is probably one of the most effective treatments available for OA of the lower limbs. Strengthening and aerobic exercises also have beneficial effects.

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: Outline the step-wise pharmacological management of Osteoarthritis if paracetamol provides inadequate relief.
back: 1. Add topical NSAIDs/Capsaicin (hand/knee). 2. Transition to oral NSAIDs (more effective). 3. Strong opiates or anti-neuropathic drugs (if control is poor).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1077 (Book Page): If symptoms do not respond to non-pharmacological measures, paracetamol should be tried. Addition of a topical NSAID and then capsaicin... Oral NSAIDs should be considered in patients who remain symptomatic.

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: Contrast the preferred acute gout management in elderly patients with comorbidities versus younger healthy patients.
back: Elderly: Joint aspiration and intra-articular glucocorticoids (avoids toxicity). Younger: Colchicine (0.5mg 2-4x daily) or oral NSAIDs.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1080 (Book Page): [Box 26.43] Acute attacks are best treated by aspiration and intra-articular injection of glucocorticoids... Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and colchicine should be used with caution because of increased risk of toxicity.

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: A patient presents with acute monoarthritis and fever. What is the immediate empirical management before culture results return?
back: 1. Hospital admission and joint aspiration. 2. IV Flucloxacillin (2g 4x daily) to cover Staphylococcus aureus. 3. Serial needle aspiration to dryness.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1084 (Book Page): Flucloxacillin (2 g IV 4 times daily) is the antibiotic of first choice pending the results of cultures... Perform serial needle aspiration to dryness (1–3 times daily).

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: What is the recommended step-up management for a Rheumatoid Arthritis patient failing Methotrexate monotherapy (DAS28 ≥ 3.2)?
back: Triple Therapy: Combine Methotrexate (MTX) with Sulfasalazine (SSZ) and Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1091 (Book Page): [Fig. 26.38] DAS28 ≥ 3.2 Add SSZ and HCQ... A common combination is triple therapy, in which MTX, SSZ and HCQ are combined.

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: List the indications for initiating urate-lowering therapy (ULT) in patients with gout.
back: >1 attack within 12 months, Tophaceous gout, Bone/joint damage on X-ray, Renal impairment, or Urate nephrolithiasis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1081 (Book Page): [Box 26.44] Recurrent attacks... Evidence of bone or joint damage... Tophi... Renal impairment... Nephrolithiasis.

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: How is a hypertensive renal crisis managed in a patient with Systemic Sclerosis?
back: Aggressive emergency administration of ACE inhibitors (even if baseline renal function is impaired).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1102 (Book Page): Aggressive treatment with ACE inhibitors is needed, even if renal impairment is present.

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: Outline the induction therapy for organ-threatening Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (e.g., Lupus Nephritis).
back: Pulsed IV Methylprednisolone (10 mg/kg) plus IV Cyclophosphamide (15 mg/kg) or Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1100 (Book Page): A commonly used regimen is pulsed methylprednisolone... plus cyclophosphamide... MMF has been used successfully... for renal involvement.

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: Describe the titration goal and physiological mechanism of Allopurinol in chronic gout.
back: Mechanism: Xanthine oxidase inhibition (reduces uric acid production). Titration Goal: Target Serum Urate < 300 μmol/L (5 mg/dL) to allow crystal dissolution.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1081 (Book Page): Allopurinol... inhibits xanthine oxidase... reducing the conversion... to uric acid. A therapeutic target of < 300 μmol/L (5 mg/dL) is recommended.

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: What are the primary pharmacological and non-pharmacological pillars of Fibromyalgia management?
back: Pharm: Low-dose Amitriptyline (encourages delta sleep). Non-Pharm: Patient education, graded aerobic exercise, and Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1084 (Book Page): Low-dose amitriptyline... encourage delta sleep... A graded increase in aerobic exercise... cognitive behavioural approach with relaxation techniques.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: List the four most common general risk factors for the development of Osteoarthritis.
back:
1. Increasing age (strongest risk factor).
2. Obesity (especially for knees/hips).
3. Female gender (post-menopause).
4. Previous joint trauma.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Osteoarthritis (OA) is by far the most common form of arthritis and is a major cause of pain and disability in older people. . . There is a strong association between obesity and OA...]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: How does obesity contribute to OA progression beyond simple mechanical loading?
back: Release of pro-inflammatory cytokines from adipose tissue (adipokines) plays a metabolic role in cartilage degradation and systemic inflammation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [This is thought to be due partly to biomechanical factors, but it has also been speculated that cytokines released from adipose tissue may play a role.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Which structural developmental abnormalities in the hip are significant risk factors for early-onset OA?
back:
• Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH).
• Slipped femoral epiphysis.
Both cause abnormal load distribution across the joint surface.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Structural abnormalities, such as slipped femoral epiphysis and developmental dysplasia of the hip, are also associated with a high risk of OA, presumably due to abnormal load distribution...]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: A 55-year-old farmer presents with chronic groin pain. Which joint and occupational risk factor is most likely?
back: Hip Osteoarthritis. Farming is a recognized occupational risk factor for hip OA due to repetitive biomechanical loading.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Biomechanical factors play an important role in OA related to certain occupations, such as farmers (hip OA), miners (knee OA)...]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: What specific pharmacological therapy for breast cancer is associated with a flare in OA symptoms?
back: Aromatase inhibitor therapy. Estrogen appears protective; its reduction via these drugs or menopause worsens symptoms.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [women who receive aromatase inhibitor therapy for breast cancer often experience a flare in symptoms of OA.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Identify the three specific 'destabilising' joint injuries that lead to a high risk of knee OA.
back:
1. Cruciate ligament rupture.
2. Meniscectomy.
3. Major intra-articular trauma.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [There is also a high risk of knee OA in people who have had destabilising injuries, such as cruciate ligament rupture, and those who have had meniscectomy.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Why does Paget's disease of the bone increase the risk of developing secondary Osteoarthritis?
back: Limb deformity secondary to Paget's disease alters joint biomechanics, leading to abnormal mechanical stress and secondary joint degeneration.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Similar mechanisms probably explain the increased risk of OA in patients with limb deformity secondary to Paget’s disease of bone.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: A patient with knee OA has pain disproportionate to X-ray findings. What physical factor correlates most strongly with pain?
back: Reduced quadriceps muscle strength. Weakness increases joint instability and is a major risk factor for pain and disability.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1074 (Book Page): [At the knee, for example, reduced quadriceps muscle strength... correlate more strongly with pain and disability than the degree of radiographic change.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: How do South and East Asian cultural habits specifically influence the prevalence of knee Osteoarthritis?
back: Repetitive squatting is thought to account for the higher prevalence of knee OA in these regions due to prolonged mechanical stress.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [It has been speculated that the higher prevalence of knee OA in South and East Asia might be accounted for by squatting.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: What is the genetic risk for a daughter if her mother has Generalized Nodal Osteoarthritis?
back: A 1 in 3 chance of developing nodal OA herself, reflecting a very strong polygenic genetic component.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1074 (Book Page): [Generalised nodal OA has a very strong genetic component: the daughter of an affected mother has a 1 in 3 chance of developing nodal OA herself.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: Outline the initial pharmacological management plan for a new diagnosis of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA).
back: 1. Promptly start cDMARDs (Methotrexate is first choice, titrated to 25mg/week). 2. Prednisolone bridging therapy (30mg daily, tapered over 12 weeks). 3. Folic acid supplementation (5mg/week).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1091 (Book Page): [On first diagnosis, prednisolone can be started in a dose of 30 mg daily gradually reducing... methotrexate (MTX) should be started in an initial dose of 15 mg weekly, along with folic acid 5 mg weekly, and escalated up to a maximum of 25 mg weekly.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: What is the core non-pharmacological management plan for a patient with knee Osteoarthritis (OA)?
back: 1. Weight loss (critical for lower limb symptoms). 2. Quadriceps muscle-strengthening and aerobic exercises. 3. Use of shock-absorbing footwear and walking sticks. 4. Pacing of activities.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1077 (Book Page): [Weight loss has a substantial beneficial effect on symptoms... Quadriceps strengthening exercises are particularly beneficial in knee OA. Shock-absorbing footwear, pacing of activities, use of a walking stick... can all improve symptoms.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: Outline the stepwise pharmacological management for pain in Osteoarthritis when non-pharmacological measures fail.
back: 1. Paracetamol (initial). 2. Addition of topical NSAIDs/Capsaicin (for hands/knees). 3. Oral NSAIDs (if symptomatic). 4. Consider strong opiates or intra-articular glucocorticoid injections.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1077 (Book Page): [If symptoms do not respond... paracetamol should be tried. Addition of a topical NSAID and then capsaicin... Oral NSAIDs should be considered... Intra-articular glucocorticoid injections are effective... for knee OA.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: Outline the emergency management plan for suspected Septic Arthritis before culture results are available.
back: 1. Admit and urgently aspirate joint for Gram stain. 2. Start IV Flucloxacillin (2g, 4x daily). 3. Switch to Vancomycin if MRSA risk exists. 4. Serial needle aspiration to dryness.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1085 (Book Page): [Aspirate joint... Flucloxacillin (2 g IV 4 times daily) is the antibiotic of first choice... If there is reason to suspect meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus... vancomycin should be used... Perform serial needle aspiration to dryness.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: Outline the pharmacological management for an acute flare of Gout.
back: 1. First-line: Oral Colchicine (0.5mg 2-4 times daily). 2. Alternative: Oral NSAIDs or Prednisolone (15-20mg daily). 3. Symptomatic: Local ice packs and joint aspiration.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1081 (Book Page): [Oral colchicine given in doses of 0.5 mg 2–4 times daily is the treatment of first choice... Oral NSAIDs are also effective... Oral prednisolone (15–20 mg daily for 2–3 days) or intramuscular methylprednisolone... are highly effective.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: How should Allopurinol be initiated and monitored in the management plan for long-term Gout prophylaxis?
back: 1. Start at 100mg daily (50mg in renal impairment). 2. Titrate by 100mg every 4 weeks until target serum urate (<300 umol/L) is reached. 3. Co-prescribe Colchicine/NSAIDs for first 6 months to prevent flares.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1081 (Book Page): [The recommended starting dose is 100 mg daily... increased by 100 mg every 4 weeks until the target uric acid level is achieved... risk of flares can be reduced by prophylaxis with oral colchicine (0.5–1 mg daily) or an NSAID.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: Outline the induction management for organ-threatening Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), such as Lupus Nephritis.
back: 1. Pulsed IV Methylprednisolone (10mg/kg). 2. Pulsed IV Cyclophosphamide (every 2 weeks for 6 cycles) OR Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF). 3. Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) for all patients.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1100 (Book Page): [High-dose glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants are required... pulsed methylprednisolone (10 mg/kg IV) plus cyclophosphamide (15 mg/kg IV)... MMF has been used successfully... for renal involvement.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: Outline the management plan for a patient presenting with suspected Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) and visual symptoms.
back: 1. Immediate Prednisolone (40-60mg daily). 2. Urgent Ophthalmology referral. 3. Temporal artery biopsy or Doppler Ultrasound (halo sign). 4. Low-dose Aspirin and Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1106 (Book Page): [Prednisolone should be commenced urgently in suspected GCA... higher doses in GCA (40–60 mg prednisolone)... Consider urgent ophthalmology examination... Consider temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: Outline the management plan for Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma) focusing on Raynaud’s and Renal Crisis.
back: 1. Raynaud's: Calcium channel blockers (Nifedipine) or IV Prostacyclin. 2. Renal Crisis: Immediate, aggressive ACE inhibitor therapy (regardless of renal function). 3. Skin: Methotrexate or MMF.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1101 (Book Page): [Raynaud's... calcium channel blockers... are effective. Hypertension. Aggressive treatment with ACE inhibitors is needed, even if renal impairment is present.]

category: Outline the management plan
front: Q: What is the management plan for Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA) according to clinical domains?
back: 1. Skin/Joints: Methotrexate (first choice). 2. Resistant Joints: Biologics (Anti-TNF, IL-17 inhibitors like Secukinumab, or IL-23 inhibitors). 3. Spondylitis: NSAIDs and physiotherapy.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1097 (Book Page): [MTX is the drug of first choice and is also effective for skin disease... Anti-TNF-α should be considered... Secukinumab and ixekizumab... have similar or even greater efficacy than TNF-α inhibitors in PsA.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: What are the primary modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors for the development of osteoarthritis?
back: Modifiable: Obesity, repetitive occupational loading, and joint trauma. Non-modifiable: Advancing age, female gender, genetic predisposition, and developmental joint abnormalities.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [OA is a complex disorder, with both genetic and environmental components... There is a strong association between obesity and OA, particularly of the hip and knee.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Through which two specific mechanisms does obesity contribute to the progression of osteoarthritis?
back:
1. Biomechanical: Increased mechanical loading on weight-bearing joints.
2. Metabolic: Systemic release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (adipokines) from adipose tissue.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [This is thought to be due partly to biomechanical factors, but it has also been speculated that cytokines released from adipose tissue may play a role.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Contrast the prevalence of hip versus knee osteoarthritis in South Asian populations compared to Europeans.
back: South Asians have a significantly lower prevalence of hip osteoarthritis but a higher prevalence of knee osteoarthritis compared to European populations.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [the prevalence of hip OA is lower in Africa, China, Japan and South Asia than in European countries, while that of knee OA is higher.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: A 50-year-old heavy laborer presents with chronic knee pain. Which occupational risk factors are relevant?
back: Repetitive loading associated with occupations like mining (knee) or farming (hip) significantly increases the risk of site-specific osteoarthritis development.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Biomechanical factors play an important role in OA related to certain occupations, such as farmers (hip OA), miners (knee OA) and elite or professional athletes.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: How do oestrogen status and aromatase inhibitor therapy affect osteoarthritis symptoms in women?
back: Oestrogen is protective; deficiency (post-menopause) increases risk, while aromatase inhibitors used in breast cancer treatment often trigger symptom flares.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Oestrogen appears important; lower rates of OA have been observed in women who use hormone replacement therapy (HRT), while women who receive aromatase inhibitor therapy for breast cancer often experience a flare.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: What is the estimated genetic heritability of osteoarthritis for the hip and hand joints?
back: Heritability is significantly high, estimated at approximately 60% for the hip and 65% for the hand joints.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [herit-ability of OA ranges from about 43% at the knee to between 60% and 65% at the hip and hand, respectively.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Which developmental joint abnormalities are major risk factors for the early onset of hip osteoarthritis?
back: Slipped femoral epiphysis and developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) lead to abnormal joint load distribution, promoting early degeneration.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Structural abnormalities, such as slipped femoral epiphysis and developmental dysplasia of the hip, are also associated with a high risk of OA, presumably due to abnormal load distribution.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Why does Paget’s disease of bone predispose a patient to developing secondary osteoarthritis?
back: Limb deformities caused by Paget’s disease alter joint alignment, creating adverse biomechanics and excessive stress on articular surfaces.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Similar mechanisms probably explain the increased risk of OA in patients with limb deformity secondary to Paget’s disease of bone. Biomechanical factors play an important role.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: What is the clinical significance of a history of meniscectomy or cruciate ligament rupture in knee OA?
back: These are high-risk biomechanical factors that cause joint instability, leading to accelerated articular cartilage degeneration and progressive osteoarthritis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [There is also a high risk of knee OA in people who have had destabilising injuries, such as cruciate ligament rupture, and those who have had meniscectomy.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Which demographic factor shows the most consistent progressive rise in osteoarthritis prevalence globally?
back: Advancing age is the most significant factor; prevalence rises progressively, with 45% of people developing knee OA in their lifetime.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [The prevalence rises progressively with age and it has been estimated that 45% of all people develop knee OA and 25% hip OA at some point during life.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: What is the most significant demographic risk factor for the development of Osteoarthritis?
back: Ageing (prevalence rises progressively with age; 45% lifetime risk for knee OA).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): The prevalence rises progressively with age and it has been estimated that 45% of all people develop knee OA and 25% hip OA at some point during life.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Besides mechanical loading, what biochemical mechanism links obesity to Osteoarthritis progression?
back: Release of pro-inflammatory cytokines from adipose tissue.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): This is thought to be due partly to biomechanical factors, but it has also been speculated that cytokines released from adipose tissue may play a role.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: How does the ethnic distribution of Osteoarthritis in South Asians differ from Europeans?
back: South Asians have a higher prevalence of knee OA but a lower prevalence of hip OA.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): the prevalence of hip OA is lower in Africa, China, Japan and South Asia than in European countries, while that of knee OA is higher.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Match these occupations to their high-risk OA sites: Farmers, Miners, and Elite Athletes.
back: 1. Farmers: Hip OA. 2. Miners: Knee OA. 3. Elite Athletes: Knee and Ankle OA.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): Biomechanical factors play an important role in OA related to certain occupations, such as farmers (hip OA), miners (knee OA) and elite or professional athletes (knee and ankle OA).

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Which hormonal deficiency and which specific oncology drug class are associated with OA flares?
back: 1. Estrogen deficiency. 2. Aromatase inhibitors (used in breast cancer).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): Oestrogen appears important; lower rates of OA have been observed in women who use hormone replacement therapy (HRT), while women who receive aromatase inhibitor therapy for breast cancer often experience a flare.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: List the four primary pathological hallmarks that define Osteoarthritis.
back: 1. Focal loss of articular cartilage. 2. Subchondral osteosclerosis. 3. Osteophyte formation. 4. Joint contour remodeling.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): It is characterised by focal loss of articular cartilage, subchondral osteosclerosis, osteophyte formation at the joint margin and remodelling of joint contour with enlargement of affected joints.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Why do developmental abnormalities like Slipped Femoral Epiphysis increase OA risk?
back: They cause abnormal distribution of mechanical load across the joint.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): Slipped femoral epiphysis and developmental dysplasia of the hip, are also associated with a high risk of OA, presumably due to abnormal load distribution across the joint.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Which two common surgical/traumatic knee events carry a high risk for subsequent OA development?
back: 1. Cruciate ligament rupture. 2. Meniscectomy.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): There is also a high risk of knee OA in people who have had destabilising injuries, such as cruciate ligament rupture, and those who have had meniscectomy.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: During OA progression, which two structural matrix components undergo accelerated degradation?
back: Aggrecan and Type II Collagen.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): at the same time there is accelerated degradation of the major structural components of cartilage matrix, including aggrecan and type II collagen.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: What is the estimated heritability of Osteoarthritis at the hip and hand sites?
back: Between 60% and 65%.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): heritability of OA ranges from about 43% at the knee to between 60% and 65% at the hip and hand, respectively.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: List four modifiable risk factors contributing to the development or progression of Osteoarthritis (OA).
back:
1. Obesity (major factor for hip/knee)
2. Repetitive joint loading (occupational)
3. Joint trauma (e.g., cruciate ligament rupture)
4. Oestrogen deficiency (hormonal)
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Box 26.36 Risk factors for osteoarthritis] Adverse biomechanics, Obesity, Trauma, Hormonal: Oestrogen deficiency... There is a strong association between obesity and OA, particularly of the hip [and] knee.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Name three specific developmental or structural abnormalities that predispose to secondary Osteoarthritis.
back:
1. Developmental dysplasia of the hip
2. Slipped femoral epiphysis
3. Limb deformity secondary to Paget’s disease of bone
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): Structural abnormalities, such as slipped femoral epiphysis and developmental dysplasia of the hip, are also associated with a high risk of OA... increased risk of OA in patients with limb deformity secondary to Paget’s disease of bone.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: How does obesity contribute to both the development and systemic progression of Osteoarthritis?
back:
1. Biomechanical: Increased mechanical loading on weight-bearing joints.
2. Biochemical: Release of pro-inflammatory cytokines from adipose tissue.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): There is a strong association between obesity and OA... This is thought to be due partly to biomechanical factors, but it has also been speculated that cytokines released from adipose tissue may play a role.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: How does age significantly impact the risk of developing Osteoarthritis (OA)?
back: Prevalence rises progressively with age; lifetime risk is estimated at 45% for knee OA and 25% for hip OA.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): The prevalence rises progressively with age and it has been estimated that 45% of all people develop knee OA and 25% hip OA at some point during life.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Identify the specific occupations and their associated high-risk joints for Osteoarthritis.
back:
• Farmers: Hip OA
• Miners: Knee OA
• Elite/Professional Athletes: Knee and Ankle OA
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): Biomechanical factors play an important role in OA related to certain occupations, such as farmers (hip OA), miners (knee OA) and elite or professional athletes (knee and ankle OA).

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: What role does estrogen status play in the development of Osteoarthritis in women?
back:
• Deficiency: Increases risk (especially post-menopause).
• HRT: Protective effect (lower OA rates).
• Depletion: Aromatase inhibitors flare OA symptoms.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): Oestrogen appears important; lower rates of OA have been observed in women who use hormone replacement therapy (HRT), while women who receive aromatase inhibitor therapy... often experience a flare in symptoms of OA.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: List the two major developmental structural abnormalities that predispose to early hip OA.
back:
• Slipped femoral epiphysis
• Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)
• Both cause abnormal load distribution across the joint.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): Structural abnormalities, such as slipped femoral epiphysis and developmental dysplasia of the hip, are also associated with a high risk of OA, presumably due to abnormal load distribution across the joint.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: How does obesity contribute to both the development and progression of Osteoarthritis?
back:
• Biomechanical: Increased mechanical loading on weight-bearing joints.
• Metabolic: Release of pro-inflammatory cytokines from adipose tissue.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): This is thought to be due partly to biomechanical factors, but it has also been speculated that cytokines released from adipose tissue may play a role.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Describe the ethnic differences in OA prevalence between South Asian and European populations.
back:
• South Asians: Higher prevalence of knee OA (partly due to squatting).
• South Asians: Lower prevalence of hip OA compared to Europeans.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): the prevalence of hip OA is lower in... South Asia than in European countries, while that of knee OA is higher. It has been speculated that the higher prevalence of knee OA in South and East Asia might be accounted for by squatting.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Why does Paget’s disease of bone increase the risk of developing OA?
back: It causes limb deformity, which creates adverse biomechanical forces across the joint surfaces.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): Similar mechanisms probably explain the increased risk of OA in patients with limb deformity secondary to Paget’s disease of bone.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: An athlete presents with knee pain after a meniscectomy. Why are they at high risk for OA?
back: Meniscectomies and cruciate ligament ruptures are 'destabilising injuries' that alter joint mechanics and accelerate cartilage degeneration.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): There is also a high risk of knee OA in people who have had destabilising injuries, such as cruciate ligament rupture, and those who have had meniscectomy.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: How do aromatase inhibitors used in breast cancer treatment affect OA progression?
back: They deplete estrogen levels, which leads to increased OA symptom flares and joint pain.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): while women who receive aromatase inhibitor therapy for breast cancer often experience a flare in symptoms of OA.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: What is the estimated heritability of hand and hip Osteoarthritis?
back:
• Hand OA: 65%
• Hip OA: 60%
• Inherited primarily through polygenic variants of small effect.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): Family-based studies have estimated that the heritability of OA ranges from about 43% at the knee to between 60% and 65% at the hip and hand, respectively.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: What are the primary epidemiological risk factors regarding age and ethnic distribution for Knee OA?
back:
• Prevalence increases progressively with age.
• High prevalence: South and East Asian populations.
• Lower prevalence: European countries (relative to hip OA).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): The prevalence rises progressively with age... the prevalence of hip OA is lower in Africa, China, Japan and South Asia than in European countries, while that of knee OA is higher.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: How does obesity contribute to both the development and progression of Knee/Hip Osteoarthritis?
back:
• Biomechanical: Increased mechanical loading on joints.
• Biochemical: Pro-inflammatory cytokines (adipokines) released from adipose tissue promote cartilage degradation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): There is a strong association between obesity and OA... due partly to biomechanical factors, but it has also been speculated that cytokines released from adipose tissue may play a role.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Which specific hormonal factors are associated with an increased risk or flare of Osteoarthritis symptoms?
back:
• Oestrogen deficiency (post-menopause).
• Aromatase inhibitor therapy (used in breast cancer treatment).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): Oestrogen appears important; lower rates of OA have been observed in women who use HRT, while women who receive aromatase inhibitor therapy for breast cancer often experience a flare.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Identify the specific joint sites most vulnerable to OA in farmers, miners, and elite athletes.
back:
• Farmers: Hip OA.
• Miners: Knee OA.
• Elite Athletes: Knee and Ankle OA.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): Biomechanical factors play an important role in OA related to certain occupations, such as farmers (hip OA), miners (knee OA) and elite or professional athletes (knee and ankle OA).

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: List three developmental or structural hip abnormalities that serve as risk factors for early-onset OA.
back:
• Slipped femoral epiphysis.
• Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH).
• Paget’s disease (due to limb deformity/abnormal loading).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): Structural abnormalities, such as slipped femoral epiphysis and developmental dysplasia of the hip... increased risk of OA in patients with limb deformity secondary to Paget’s disease.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Which specific knee joint injuries are major contributors to the long-term development of Osteoarthritis?
back:
• Cruciate ligament rupture.
• Meniscectomy (surgical removal of the meniscus).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): There is also a high risk of knee OA in people who have had destabilising injuries, such as cruciate ligament rupture, and those who have had meniscectomy.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: How does systemic Bone Mineral Density (BMD) relate to the risk of developing Osteoarthritis?
back:
• High BMD is positively associated with OA (especially osteophyte formation).
• Patients with OA are often partially protected from developing osteoporosis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1074 (Book Page): Patients with OA also have higher BMD values... this is in keeping with observations... that show that patients with OA are partially protected from developing osteoporosis.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: What cultural biomechanical habit is associated with the increased prevalence of Knee OA in Asian regions?
back: • Squatting (associated with repetitive, high-load biomechanical stress on the knee).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): It has been speculated that the higher prevalence of knee OA in South and East Asia might be accounted for by squatting.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: Which secondary crystal deposition accelerates the progression of established Osteoarthritis?
back:
• Calcium Pyrophosphate (CPP) crystals.
• Associated with increased inflammation (effusions/stiffness) and more rapid radiographic deterioration.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1075 (Book Page): CPP crystal deposition in association with OA... may be associated with more rapid radiographic and clinical progression.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Q: What is the genetic heritability of OA at the hip and hand joints compared to the knee?
back:
• Hip and Hand: 60%–65%.
• Knee: 43%.
• Generally polygenic inheritance.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): heritability of OA ranges from about 43% at the knee to between 60% and 65% at the hip and hand, respectively. In most cases, the inheritance is polygenic.

category: Describe the clinical features and typical pattern of joint involvement in OA
front: Q: What are the four defining pathological hallmarks of Osteoarthritis (OA)?
back:
• Focal loss of articular cartilage
• Subchondral osteosclerosis
• Osteophyte formation at joint margins
• Remodelling and enlargement of affected joints
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): Osteoarthritis (OA) is... characterised by focal loss of articular cartilage, subchondral osteosclerosis, osteophyte formation at the joint margin and remodelling of joint contour with enlargement of affected joints.

category: Describe the clinical features and typical pattern of joint involvement in OA
front: Q: Describe the characteristic joint distribution of Osteoarthritis in the body.
back:
OA primarily targets:
• Hips and Knees
• PIP and DIP joints of the hands
• Cervical and Lumbar spine
• First carpometacarpal (CMC) joint
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1074 (Book Page): Osteoarthritis has a characteristic distribution, mainly targeting the hips, knees, PIP and DIP joints of the hands, neck and lumbar spine.

category: Describe the clinical features and typical pattern of joint involvement in OA
front: Q: What defines the duration of morning stiffness and 'gelling' in Osteoarthritis?
back:
• Morning stiffness: Typically lasts < 15 minutes
• Inactivity 'gelling': Usually lasts < 5 minutes after rest
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1074 (Book Page): Mild morning stiffness ( < 15 mins) and inactivity gelling ( < 5 mins) after rest.

category: Describe the clinical features and typical pattern of joint involvement in OA
front: Q: A 60-year-old female presents with pain at the thumb base. What clinical signs suggest OA?
back:
• Crepitus on joint movement
• 'Squaring' of the thumb base (first CMC joint involvement)
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1074 (Book Page): Involvement of the rst carpometacarpal (CMC) joint is also common... detected by the presence of crepitus on joint movement and squaring of the thumb base.

category: Describe the clinical features and typical pattern of joint involvement in OA
front: Q: Name the specific bony nodes associated with the DIP and PIP joints in OA.
back:
• Heberden's nodes: Distal Interphalangeal (DIP) joints
• Bouchard's nodes: Proximal Interphalangeal (PIP) joints
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1074 (Book Page): ...slowly enlarge and harden to become Heberden’s (DIP) and Bouchard’s (PIP) nodes.

category: Describe the clinical features and typical pattern of joint involvement in OA
front: Q: List four clinical signs found on local examination of an OA joint.
back:
• Palpable or audible coarse crepitus
• Bony swelling around margins
• Restricted movement
• Muscle weakness and wasting
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1074 (Book Page): Restricted movement... Palpable, sometimes audible, coarse crepitus... Bony swelling around joint margins... Muscle weakness and wasting.

category: Describe the clinical features and typical pattern of joint involvement in OA
front: Q: What are the primary compartments of the knee targeted by OA and the resulting deformity?
back:
• Compartments: Patello-femoral and medial tibio-femoral
• Common Deformity: Varus deformity (bow-legged)
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1074 (Book Page): OA principally targets the patello-femoral and medial tibio-femoral compartments... Local examination ndings may include: a varus... deformity.

category: Describe the clinical features and typical pattern of joint involvement in OA
front: Q: A patient complains of deep groin pain radiating to the thigh. Which sign is most sensitive for Hip OA?
back: • Pain and restriction of internal rotation while the hip is flexed.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1076 (Book Page): pain and restriction of internal rotation with the hip exed – the earliest and most sensitive sign of hip OA.

category: Describe the clinical features and typical pattern of joint involvement in OA
front: Q: Describe the typical pain pattern in Osteoarthritis regarding activity.
back:
• Insidious onset
• Related to movement and weight-bearing
• Relieved by rest
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1074 (Book Page): Pain: Insidious onset over months or years... Mainly related to movement and weight-bearing, relieved by rest.

category: Describe the clinical features and typical pattern of joint involvement in OA
front: Q: What defines 'Erosive OA' as a distinct subset of hand OA?
back:
• Preferential targeting of PIP joints
• Subchondral erosions on X-ray
• Overt inflammation and possible ankylosis
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1076 (Book Page): Erosive OA... Distinguishing features include preferential targeting of PIP joints, subchondral erosions on X-rays, occasional ankylosis of affected joints.

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: How do advancing age and gender influence the lifetime risk of developing knee versus hip osteoarthritis?
back: Risk rises progressively with age. Lifetime risk is estimated at 45% for knee OA and 25% for hip OA, with higher rates in women.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [The prevalence rises progressively with age and it has been estimated that 45% of all people develop knee OA and 25% hip OA at some point during life. ... the lifetime risk of having a total hip or knee replacement for OA in someone aged 50 is about 11% for women and 8% for men in the UK.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Compare the estimated heritability rates of osteoarthritis for the hip, hand, and knee joints.
back:
• Hip: 60%–65%
• Hand: 60%–65%
• Knee: 43%
Inheritance is typically polygenic with variants of small effect.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Family-based studies have estimated that the heritability of OA ranges from about 43% at the knee to between 60% and 65% at the hip and hand, respectively.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Which childhood structural abnormalities predispose to early-onset hip osteoarthritis due to abnormal joint loading?
back:
• Slipped femoral epiphysis
• Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)
Both cause abnormal load distribution across the joint surface.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Structural abnormalities, such as slipped femoral epiphysis and developmental dysplasia of the hip, are also associated with a high risk of OA, presumably due to abnormal load distribution across the joint.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
coreConcept: Metabolic and Biomechanical Risks of Obesity
front: Identify the primary mechanism linking obesity to the development and progression of knee and hip OA.
back:
1. Biomechanical: Increased mechanical load on joints.
2. Metabolic: Release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (adipokines) from adipose tissue.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [There is a strong association between obesity and OA, particularly of the hip knee. This is thought to be due partly to biomechanical factors, but it has also been speculated that cytokines released from adipose tissue may play a role.]

category: Identify risk factors for contributing to the development and progression of osteoarthritis
front: Link the following occupations to their high-risk specific site for osteoarthritis: Farmers vs. Miners.
back:
• Farmers: High risk for Hip OA.
• Miners: High risk for Knee OA.
Athletes are at higher risk for Knee and Ankle OA.
