citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1040 (Book Page): [Cyclophosphamide may cause haemorrhagic cystitis, but the risk can be minimised by good hydration and co-prescription of mesna]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Define the constituents of 'Triple Therapy' used in RA when Methotrexate monotherapy fails.
back:
• Methotrexate (MTX).
• Sulfasalazine (SSZ).
• Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1031 (Book Page): [A common combination is triple therapy, in which MTX, SSZ and HCQ are combined]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Beyond antibiotics, what is the essential procedural management for an acutely inflamed septic joint?
back:
• Urgent joint aspiration to dryness.
• Serial needle aspiration (1–3 times daily) or arthroscopic drainage if needed.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1025 (Book Page): [The principles of management are... Joint aspiration should be performed using a large-bore needle once or twice daily. If this is not possible, arthroscopic or open surgical drainage may be needed.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: How is 'non-restorative sleep' specifically managed pharmacologically in Fibromyalgia patients?
back:
• Low-dose Amitriptyline (10–75 mg at night).
• Encourages delta sleep and reduces spinal cord wind-up.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1024 (Book Page): [Low-dose amitriptyline (10–75 mg at night)... may help by encouraging delta sleep and reducing spinal cord wind-up.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Why is antibiotic therapy alone usually insufficient for management of infected prosthetic joints?
back:
• Biofilm/sequestration makes antibiotics ineffective.
• Removal of the prosthesis is usually required to eradicate infection.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1026 (Book Page): [Infected prosthetic joints require management by the orthopaedic team, but prolonged antibiotic treatment on its own is often ineffective and removal of the prosthesis may be required]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Outline the supportive management for gastroesophageal reflux in Systemic Sclerosis (SScl).
back:
• High-dose Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs).
• Anti-reflux agents (Alginates).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1042 (Book Page): [Oesophageal reflux should be treated with proton pump inhibitors and anti-reflux agents.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Which specific immunosuppressants are prioritized when Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) is complicated by uveitis?
back:
• Methotrexate (standard).
• Azathioprine or Ciclosporin.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1032 (Book Page): [AZA and ciclosporin can be used to treat JIA with uveitis. MMF and tacrolimus are considered to have a specific role in treating uveitis alone.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Which human IL-1 receptor antagonist is primarily used to treat adult-onset Still’s disease?
back: Anakinra. It neutralizes the effects of IL-1α and IL-1β by inhibiting their binding to the interleukin-1 type I receptor.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Anakinra is a human IL-1 receptor antagonist... Its most frequent use is for the treatment of adult-onset Still’s disease]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: What major adverse risk is associated with IL-17A inhibitors used in Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA) and axSpA?
back: An increased risk of triggering or exacerbating Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), alongside nasopharyngitis and headache.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Adverse effects include an increased risk of triggering bouts of IBD, infections, nasopharyngitis and headache.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Outline the standard starting dose and escalation protocol for Methotrexate (MTX) in Rheumatoid Arthritis.
back:
• Start: 15 mg weekly
• Co-therapy: 5 mg folic acid weekly
• Maximize: Escalate up to 25 mg weekly based on response.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1091 (Book Page): [methotrexate (MTX) should be started in an initial dose of 15 mg weekly, along with folic acid 5 mg weekly, and escalated up to a maximum of 25 mg weekly]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: What is the life-saving pharmacological intervention for managing hypertensive renal crisis in Systemic Sclerosis (SScl)?
back: Aggressive treatment with ACE inhibitors. They are mandatory even if renal impairment is already present.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1102 (Book Page): [Aggressive treatment with ACE inhibitors is needed, even if renal impairment is present.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Compare the initial Prednisolone dosing for Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) versus Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR).
back:
• GCA: 40–60 mg daily (high dose to prevent blindness).
• PMR: 15–20 mg daily.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1106 (Book Page): [It is customary to use higher doses in GCA (40–60 mg prednisolone) than in PMR (15–20 mg).]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: List the four clinical and laboratory components used to calculate the DAS28 in RA patients.
back:
1. Swollen joint count
2. Tender joint count
3. ESR or CRP levels
4. Patient global health assessment (Visual Analogue Scale).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1090 (Book Page): [It involves counting the number of swollen and tender joints... combining this with the ESR and the patient’s assessment of the activity of their arthritis on a visual analogue scale]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: How does Pegloticase reduce urate in resistant gout, and what is its primary clinical limitation?
back:
• Mechanism: Breaks down uric acid using the enzyme uricase.
• Limitation: Frequent development of anti-pegloticase antibodies, which impairs therapeutic efficacy.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1081 (Book Page): [It breaks down uric acid... A limiting factor for longer-term treatment is the development of antibodies to pegloticase... associated with an impaired therapeutic response.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Identify the first-line pharmacotherapy combination used to prevent coronary aneurysms in Kawasaki disease.
back: Aspirin (5 mg/kg/day) combined with Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIg) (400 mg/kg/day for 5 days).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1105 (Book Page): [Treatment is with aspirin (5 mg/kg daily for 14 days) and IVIg (400 mg/kg daily for 5 days).]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: What is the preferred standard DMARD and its typical route of administration for young children with JIA?
back: Methotrexate (MTX). In young children, it is typically administered via the subcutaneous route.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1092 (Book Page): [Standard therapy is MTX (subcutaneous MTX is typically used in the young child).]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: When are intra-articular glucocorticoid injections specifically indicated for the management of Osteoarthritis (OA)?
back: Used for short-term symptomatic relief of the knee or first CMC joint, often to tide a patient over special events.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1076 (Book Page): [Intra-articular injection of glucocorticoid... particularly useful for tiding a patient over a special event.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: What is the immediate first-line pharmacological management for suspected Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA)?
back:
- Prednisolone (40–60 mg daily).
- Start urgently to prevent irreversible visual loss.
- Response is typically dramatic within 48–72 hours.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1106 (Book Page): [Prednisolone should be commenced urgently in suspected GCA because of the risk of visual loss... 40–60 mg daily]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Explain the pharmacological mechanism and clinical target for Allopurinol in gout management.
back:
- Mechanism: Inhibits xanthine oxidase.
- Effect: Reduces conversion of hypoxanthine/xanthine to uric acid.
- Clinical Target: Serum Urate <300 μmol/L.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1081 (Book Page): [It inhibits xanthine oxidase, which reduces the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid. The recommended starting dose is 100 mg daily... until the target uric acid level is achieved]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Why is weight loss prioritized in the non-pharmacological management of lower-limb Osteoarthritis?
back:
- Substantial beneficial effect on symptoms.
- One of the most effective treatments for hip and knee OA.
- Reduces biomechanical load on failing joints.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1077 (Book Page): [Weight loss has a substantial beneficial effect on symptoms if the patient is obese and is probably one of the most effective treatments available for OA of the lower limbs.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: A 60-year-old with a hot, swollen knee and suspected Septic Arthritis requires which empirical antibiotic?
back:
- Flucloxacillin (2g IV 4 times daily).
- Pending culture results.
- Covers common Staphylococcal and Streptococcal infections.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1085 (Book Page): [Flucloxacillin (2 g IV 4 times daily) is the antibiotic of  first choice pending the results of cultures, since it will cover most staphylococcal and streptococcal infections.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Identify the specific pharmacological target and clinical use of Anakinra in rheumatology.
back:
- Target: Human IL-1 receptor antagonist.
- Indications: Adult-onset Still’s disease, periodic fever syndromes, and resistant acute gout flares.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1073 (Book Page): [Anakinra is a human IL-1 receptor antagonist... Its most frequent use is for the treatment of adult-onset Still’s disease and for periodic fever syndromes]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: What is the gold-standard first-line cDMARD for newly diagnosed Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)?
back:
- Methotrexate (MTX) weekly.
- Co-prescribe Folic Acid (5 mg weekly).
- Escalated from 15 mg to maximum 25 mg weekly.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1091 (Book Page): [methotrexate (MTX) should be started in an initial dose of 15 mg weekly, along with folic acid 5 mg weekly, and escalated up to a maximum of 25 mg weekly]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Which specific class of drugs is mandatory for managing a Systemic Sclerosis (SSc) hypertensive renal crisis?
back:
- ACE Inhibitors.
- Required even if renal impairment is already present.
- Manages the accelerated phase hypertension hallmark.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1101 (Book Page): [Aggressive treatment with ACE inhibitors is needed, even if renal impairment is present.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: How is the acute management of gout modified for elderly patients or those with renal impairment?
back:
- Prefer: Aspiration and intra-articular glucocorticoids.
- Alternative: Low-dose oral steroids.
- Caution: Avoid NSAIDs and Colchicine due to toxicity risk.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1080 (Book Page): [acute attacks are best treated by aspiration and intra-articular injection of glucocorticoids... Non-steroidal anti-in ammatory drugs and colchicine should be used with caution because of increased risk of toxicity.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: What pharmacological and lifestyle combination is recommended for managing non-restorative sleep in Fibromyalgia?
back:
- Low-dose Amitriptyline (10–75 mg at night).
- Graded aerobic exercise to improve well-being and sleep quality.
- Addressing psychological distress.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1084 (Book Page): [Low-dose amitriptyline (10–75 mg at night)... A graded increase in aerobic exercise can improve well-being and sleep quality.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Outline the initial pharmacological regimen for managing Osteoarticular Tuberculosis (Pott’s Disease).
back:
- Quadruple therapy: Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide, and Ethambutol.
- Duration: 2 months for the initial phase.
- Total treatment can extend to 12–18 months.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1087 (Book Page): [quadruple therapy with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol should be given as  first-line therapy for 2 months and followed by 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What are the primary general complications resulting from systemic inflammatory vasculitis?
back:
- Local tissue ischaemia due to vessel narrowing.
- Multi-organ failure from inflammation.
- Constitutional symptoms like fever and weight loss.
- Chronic organ damage (e.g., renal or pulmonary).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): [The clinical features result from a combination of local tissue ischaemia (due to vessel inflammation and narrowing) and the systemic effects of widespread inflammation. Systemic vasculitis should be considered in any patient with fever, weight loss, fatigue, evidence of multisystem involvement...]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What is the most catastrophic long-term ocular outcome of untreated Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA)?
back:
- Permanent blindness in the affected eye.
- Caused by occlusion of the posterior ciliary artery.
- Occurs suddenly, often following amaurosis fugax.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1046 (Book Page): [Visual disturbance can occur (most specifically amaurosis) and a catastrophic presentation is with blindness in one eye due to occlusion of the posterior ciliary artery.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Which anatomical structures are permanently destroyed in long-standing Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA)?
back:
- Nasal bone and cartilage (causing saddle nose deformity).
- Tracheobronchial tree (subglottic stenosis).
- Orbit (leading to proptosis and optic nerve compression).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): [Untreated nasal disease ultimately leads to destruction of bone and cartilage... proptosis may occur because of inflammation of the retro-orbital tissue.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Identify the most serious long-term cardiovascular complications of Kawasaki disease in children.
back:
- Coronary artery aneurysms.
- Myocardial infarction due to coronary arteritis.
- Myocarditis or pericarditis.
- Peripheral vascular gangrene.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1045 (Book Page): [Cardiovascular complications include coronary arteritis, leading to myocardial infarction, transient coronary dilatation, myocarditis, pericarditis, peripheral vascular insufficiency and gangrene.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Differentiate the primary renal complications of Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN) versus Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA).
back:
- PAN: Multiple renal infarctions and severe hypertension; glomerulonephritis is rare.
- MPA: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): [Severe hypertension and/or renal impairment may occur due to multiple renal infarctions, but glomerulonephritis is rare (in contrast to MPA).]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: List two life-threatening complications associated with long-term cyclophosphamide use for vasculitis.
back:
- Haemorrhagic cystitis.
- Permanent infertility (azoospermia or premature menopause).
- Increased risk of bladder malignancy.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1040 (Book Page): [Cyclophosphamide may cause haemorrhagic cystitis... Because of the risk of azoospermia and premature menopause, sperm or oocyte collection and storage need to be considered...]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What neurological complications define the acute presentation of Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA)?
back:
- Asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex.
- Cranial nerve palsies.
- Potential mesenteric vasculitis causing abdominal pain.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): [The typical acute presentation is with a triad of skin lesions (purpura or nodules), asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex and eosinophilia.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Which specific malignancy is a long-term risk for patients with chronic Takayasu Arteritis?
back:
- Aortic aneurysm formation.
- Aortic incompetence/regurgitation.
- Secondary hypertension from renal artery narrowing.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1045 (Book Page): [Aortic coarctation, and aneurysmal dilatation may also occur. The diagnosis can also be made by 18 fluorodeoxyglucose PET-CT...]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Describe the long-term central nervous system outcomes associated with Behçet’s disease.
back:
- Brainstem involvement leading to pyramidal signs.
- Chronic meningitis or encephalitis.
- Cranial nerve lesions.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1047 (Book Page): [Neurological involvement occurs in 5% and mainly involves the brainstem... causing pyramidal signs, cranial nerve lesions, brainstem symptoms or hemiparesis.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What long-term monitoring parameters are essential to detect relapses in ANCA-associated vasculitis?
back:
- Serial C-reactive protein (CRP) and ESR.
- Frequent urinalysis (for hematuria/proteinuria).
- Plasma creatinine levels.
- Monitoring PR3 or MPO antibody titers.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1045 (Book Page): [Patients with AAV must be followed on a regular and long-term basis since the condition has a tendency to relapse, monitoring urinalysis for blood and protein, plasma creatinine, FBC, ESR, CRP, lung function and PR3 or MPO antibody titres.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: When should topical NSAIDs or capsaicin be used in the step-wise management of osteoarthritis?
back: They are recommended for symptomatic relief as an adjunct to paracetamol, specifically for osteoarthritis affecting the knee and hand joints.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1077 (Book Page): [Addition of a topical NSAID and then capsaicin for knee and hand OA can also be helpful.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Identify the specific clinical indications for using Febuxostat over Allopurinol in chronic gout management.
back: Indicated when there is an inadequate response to Allopurinol, or when Allopurinol is contraindicated or causes intolerable adverse effects.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1081 (Book Page): [Febuxostat... is typically used in patients with an inadequate response to allopurinol and when allopurinol is contraindicated or causes adverse effects.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Which class of medications and specific drug are used to prevent new ischemic digital ulcers in systemic sclerosis?
back: Endothelin-1 antagonists; specifically Bosentan is licensed for treating existing ulcers and preventing the recurrence of ischemic digital ulcers.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1101 (Book Page): [The endothelin-1 antagonist bosentan is licensed for treating ischaemic digital ulcers.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Why is co-treatment with Methotrexate recommended when initiating biologic therapy in Rheumatoid Arthritis patients?
back: Evidence shows that co-treatment with Methotrexate significantly enhances both the efficacy and the durability of the therapeutic response to biologics.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1091 (Book Page): [Studies show that efficacy and durability of response to biologics is enhanced by co-treatment with MTX.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Which immunosuppressive agents are specifically used for managing the uveitis associated with Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis?
back:
1. Azathioprine and Ciclosporin (standard for JIA with uveitis).
2. Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF) and Tacrolimus (specific roles in uveitis alone).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1092 (Book Page): [AZA and ciclosporin can be used to treat JIA with uveitis. MMF and tacrolimus are considered to have a specific role in treating uveitis alone.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Identify the first-line pharmacological treatment for Polymyositis and Dermatomyositis and its typical starting dose.
back: Oral glucocorticoids (Prednisolone) are first-line, typically started at a dose of 1 mg/kg daily and tapered based on response.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1103 (Book Page): [Oral glucocorticoids (prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily) are the first-line treatment of PM and DM.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Explain the unique benefit of choosing Methotrexate as the first-choice DMARD in Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA).
back: Methotrexate is highly effective at managing both the articular (joint) inflammation and the underlying cutaneous (skin) psoriatic lesions simultaneously.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1097 (Book Page): [MTX is the drug of first choice and is also effective for skin disease.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Identify the four standard steroid-sparing immunosuppressants used for maintenance therapy in Polymyositis/Dermatomyositis.
back:
1. Methotrexate (MTX).
2. Azathioprine.
3. Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF).
4. Ciclosporin.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1103 (Book Page): [additional immunosuppressive therapy may be required as steroid-sparing agents in the form of MTX, azathioprine, MMF or ciclosporin.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Which common antihypertensive medication should be prioritized for substitution in gout patients, and why?
back: Losartan should be substituted; unlike most antihypertensives, it has a beneficial uricosuric effect that helps lower serum uric acid levels.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1081 (Book Page): [whereas losartan has a uricosuric effect and should be substituted for other drugs if possible.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Outline the pharmacological management for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) and dysmotility in Systemic Sclerosis.
back:
1. SIBO: Rotating courses of oral antibiotics.
2. Dysmotility: Prokinetics like Metoclopramide or Domperidone.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1101 (Book Page): [Rotating courses of antibiotics may be required for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth... while metoclopramide or domperidone may help patients with symptoms of dysmotility.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What severe long-term structural complications occur in the upper respiratory tract due to untreated Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)?
back:
• Destruction of nasal bone and cartilage (saddle nose deformity)
• Conductive or sensory deafness
• Proptosis and orbital tissue inflammation causing vision loss
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1083 (Book Page): [Untreated nasal disease ultimately leads to destruction of bone and cartilage. ... Deafness may be a feature due to inner ear involvement and proptosis may occur because of inflammation of the retro-orbital tissue.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Differentiate the primary long-term renal outcomes of Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN) versus Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA).
back:
• PAN: Renal infarction and severe hypertension; glomerulonephritis is rare.
• MPA: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and alveolar haemorrhage.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1084 (Book Page): [Severe hypertension and/or renal impairment may occur due to multiple renal infarctions, but glomerulonephritis is rare (in contrast to MPA).]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Which neurological and respiratory sequelae are characteristic long-term outcomes of Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA)?
back:
• Chronic, difficult-to-control late-onset asthma
• Asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex (sensory/motor neuropathy)
• Mesenteric vasculitis causing abdominal complications
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1083 (Book Page): [...late-onset asthma that is often difficult to control. The typical acute presentation is with a triad of skin lesions (purpura or nodules), asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex and eosinophilia.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What are the primary vascular outcomes and long-term survival expectations for Takayasu arteritis?
back:
• Vascular: Occlusion, stenosis, or aneurysmal dilatation of the aorta/major branches
• Survival: 83% five-year survival rate with successful treatment
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1084 (Book Page): [Takayasu arteritis... characterized by granulomatous inflammation of the vessel wall, leading to its occlusion or weakening. ... With successful treatment, the 5-year survival is 83%.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Identify the potentially fatal cardiovascular complications associated with Kawasaki disease.
back:
• Coronary artery aneurysms and myocardial infarction
• Myocarditis and pericarditis
• Peripheral vascular insufficiency leading to gangrene
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1084 (Book Page): [Cardiovascular complications include coronary arteritis, leading to myocardial infarction, transient coronary dilatation, myocarditis, pericarditis, peripheral vascular insufficiency and gangrene.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What is the most catastrophic permanent complication of Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) and the vessel involved?
back:
• Permanent blindness (visual loss)
• Mechanism: Occlusion of the posterior ciliary artery
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1085 (Book Page): [A catastrophic presentation is with blindness in one eye due to occlusion of the posterior ciliary artery.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: List three severe systemic complications that define the long-term morbidity of Behçet’s disease.
back:
• Recurrent venous and arterial thromboses
• Permanent vision loss from posterior uveitis/retinal vasculitis
• Neuro-Behçet’s (brainstem involvement and pyramidal signs)
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1086 (Book Page): [Ocular involvement is common and may include anterior or posterior uveitis or retinal vasculitis. ... Neurological involvement occurs in 5% and mainly involves the brainstem ... Recurrent thromboses also occur.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: A pediatric patient presents with Henoch–Schönlein purpura (HSP). Within what timeframe can nephritis typically complicate the course?
back: • Nephritis may present up to 4 weeks after the onset of initial symptoms (purpura/abdominal pain)
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1085 (Book Page): [Nephritis can also occur and may present up to 4 weeks after the onset of other symptoms.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What is the clinical tendency of ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) that necessitates lifelong monitoring?
back:
• High tendency to relapse
• Requires long-term monitoring of ANCA titers, inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP), and renal function (urinalysis/creatinine)
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1084 (Book Page): [Patients with AAV must be followed on a regular and long-term basis since the condition has a tendency to relapse...]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Pathophysiologically, what are the two primary drivers of clinical features in systemic vasculitis?
back:
• Local tissue ischaemia (due to vessel inflammation and narrowing)
• Systemic effects resulting from widespread inflammatory mediators
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1083 (Book Page): [The clinical features result from a combination of local tissue ischaemia (due to vessel inflammation and narrowing) and the systemic effects of widespread inflammation.]

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: What is the first-line Conventional Synthetic DMARD (csDMARD) and its standard starting dose for Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back:
• Drug: Methotrexate (MTX)
• Starting dose: 15 mg weekly (oral or subcutaneous)
• Escalation: Up to 25 mg weekly
• Mandatory: Co-prescribe with Folic Acid (5 mg weekly).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1091 (Book Page): [M]ethotrexate (MTX) should be started in an initial dose of 15 mg weekly, along with folic acid 5 mg weekly, and escalated up to a maximum of 25 mg weekly, depending on the response.

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Describe the pharmacological mechanism of Allopurinol in the management of chronic gout.
back:
• Mechanism: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor
• Effect: Reduces conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid
• Goal: Lowers serum urate (SUA) to prevent crystal formation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1081 (Book Page): Allopurinol is the drug of rst choice. It inhibits xanthine oxidase, which reduces the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid.

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Contrast the primary pharmacological therapy used for an acute gout attack versus chronic prophylaxis.
back:
• Acute attack: Colchicine (0.5 mg 2–4x daily) or NSAIDs to reduce inflammation.
• Chronic prophylaxis: Allopurinol (Xanthine oxidase inhibitor) to lower serum urate.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1081 (Book Page): Oral colchicine given in doses of 0.5 mg 2–4 times daily is the tr eatment of rst choice in acute gout... Allopurinol is the drug of rst choice [for prophylaxis].

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: What is the immediate pharmacological management for a patient with suspected Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) and visual disturbance?
back:
• Urgent high-dose Prednisolone (40–60 mg daily)
• Urgent Ophthalmology referral
• Temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound confirmation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1106 (Book Page): Prednisolone should be commenced urgently in suspected GCA because of the risk of visual loss... higher doses in GCA (40–60 mg prednisolone) than in PMR.

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Which specific pharmacological class is mandatory for managing Hypertensive Renal Crisis in Systemic Sclerosis?
back:
• ACE Inhibitors (e.g., Enalapril)
• Used even if renal impairment is present
• Essential for managing accelerated phase hypertension.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1101 (Book Page): Aggressive treatment with ACE inhibitors is needed, even if renal impairment is pr esent.

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: According to the 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria, what total score classifies a patient as having 'definite' Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: • A cumulative score of ≥ 6 out of 10 points is required for classification.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1087 (Book Page): Patients with a score ≥ 6 are considered to have denite RA.

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: Outline the essential non-pharmacological supportive steps for managing acute Septic Arthritis.
back:
• Hospital admission for parenteral antibiotics
• Serial needle aspiration to dryness (1–3 times daily)
• Early regular passive movement to active movement.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1085 (Book Page): Perform serial needle aspiration to dryness (1–3 times daily or as required)... Early regular passive movement, progressing to active movements once pain controlled.

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: In an elderly patient with acute monoarthritis, how does management prioritize if both CPP crystals and Gram-positive cocci are identified?
back:
• Priority: Treat as Septic Arthritis (IV Flucloxacillin + drainage)
• Avoid: Delay intra-articular glucocorticoids until infection is ruled out
• Joint sepsis and CPPD often coexist.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1082 (Book Page): Since sepsis and acute CPP crys - tal arthritis can coexist, Gram stain and cultur e of the uid should be performed to exclude sepsis, even if CPP crystals ar e identied.

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: What is the recommended serum urate (SUA) therapeutic target for long-term gout prophylaxis?
back:
• Target: < 300 μmol/L (5 mg/dL)
• Goal: Maintain level below the threshold of monosodium urate crystal formation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1081 (Book Page): A ther - apeutic target of < 300 μmol/L (5 mg/dL) is r ecommended in the British Society of Rheumatology guidelines.

category: Outline principles of management including pharmacological and supportive therapies
front: Q: What is the pharmacological rationale and standard nighttime dose for Amitriptyline in Fibromyalgia?
back:
• Dose: 10–75 mg at night
• Rationale: Encourages delta (restorative) sleep and reduces spinal cord pain sensitization (wind-up).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1084 (Book Page): Low-dose amitriptyline (10–75 mg at night)... may help by encouraging delta sleep and r educing spinal cor d wind-up.

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What specific vascular occlusion in Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) causes catastrophic permanent visual loss?
back: Occlusion of the posterior ciliary artery. This results in optic disc swelling and pallor, often progressing to total blindness if untreated.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1046 (Book Page): [a catastrophic presentation is with blindness in one eye due to occlusion of the posterior ciliary artery.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: How does renal involvement in Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN) differ pathologically from Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA)?
back: PAN causes multiple renal infarctions and severe hypertension. Unlike MPA, glomerulonephritis is typically absent/rare in PAN.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1045 (Book Page): [Severe hypertension and/or renal impairment may occur due to multiple renal infarctions, but glomerulonephritis is rare (in contrast to MPA).]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Identify the mechanism behind proptosis and diplopia in Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA).
back: Retro-orbital inflammation/granuloma formation. This causes extra-ocular muscle entrapment or optic nerve compression leading to vision loss.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): [proptosis may occur because of inflammation of the retro-orbital tissue. This causes diplopia due to entrapment of the extra-ocular muscles, or loss of vision due to optic nerve compression.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What are the two primary long-term structural outcomes for the aorta in Takayasu Arteritis?
back:
1. Occlusion (causing limb/organ claudication).
2. Weakening (leading to aortic coarctation or aneurysmal dilatation).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1045 (Book Page): [granulomatous inflammation of the vessel wall, leading to its occlusion or weakening... Aortic coarctation, and aneurysmal dilatation may also occur.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Describe the characteristic triad of acute complications found in Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA).
back:
1. Skin lesions (purpura/nodules).
2. Asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex.
3. Eosinophilia (on background of refractory asthma).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): [The typical acute presentation is with a triad of skin lesions (purpura or nodules), asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex and eosinophilia.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Which specific complication of Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA) presents as a life-threatening pulmonary-renal syndrome?
back: Alveolar haemorrhage. It often occurs simultaneously with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): [Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) is a necrotising small-vessel vasculitis found with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, often in association with alveolar haemorrhage.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Identify the most critical long-term outcome associated with the tracheobronchial cartilage in Relapsing Polychondritis.
back: Cartilage collapse leading to hoarseness, cough, stridor, or life-threatening expiratory wheeze.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1047 (Book Page): [Involvement of tracheobronchial cartilage may lead to a hoarseness, cough, stridor or expiratory wheeze... an important cause of mortality.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What is the primary cause of blindness in patients with Behçet’s disease?
back: Retinal vasculitis. It results from repeated bouts of anterior or posterior uveitis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1106 (Book Page): [Ocular involvement is common and may include anterior or posterior uveitis or retinal vasculitis.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Describe the neurological outcomes associated with Neuro-Behçet’s disease.
back:
1. Brainstem syndromes.
2. Pyramidal signs.
3. Recurrent venous thromboses (including cerebral veins).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1106 (Book Page): [Neurological involvement occurs in 5% and mainly involves the brainstem... causing pyramidal signs... Recurrent thromboses also occur.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What four clinical parameters must be monitored long-term to detect relapses in ANCA-associated vasculitis?
back:
1. Urinalysis (blood/protein).
2. Plasma creatinine.
3. CRP/ESR/FBC.
4. ANCA titers (PR3 or MPO).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1045 (Book Page): [Patients with AAV must be followed on a regular and long-term basis... monitoring urinalysis for blood and protein, plasma creatinine, FBC, ESR, CRP and PR3 or MPO antibody titres.]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Which genetic marker is present in over 95% of patients with Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS)?
back: HLA-B27. It is the strongest genetic risk factor for the development of radiographic axial spondyloarthritis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [There is a] striking association with HLA-B27, particularly for AS (> 95%).

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Describe the primary cytokine axis responsible for the immunopathogenesis of axial spondyloarthritis.
back: The IL-23/IL-17 axis. IL-23 triggers Th17 lymphocytes to produce IL-17 and TNF-α, driving joint inflammation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [axSpA arises from] increased production of IL-23, which in turn causes activation of Th17 lymphocytes that produce IL-17, TNF-α and other inflammatory cytokines.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: What is the hallmark pathological lesion of spondyloarthritis, and where does it occur?
back: Enthesitis. It is inflammation at the specific site where a ligament or tendon inserts into bone.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): A hallmark lesion of SpAs is enthesitis, which is inflammation at the site of a ligament or tendon insertion into bone.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: List three non-HLA genetic factors that contribute to the susceptibility of Ankylosing Spondylitis.
back:
1. ERAP-1 (antigen processing)
2. IL-23 Receptor
3. STAT3 (signaling molecule).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): Other susceptibility genes also implicated in susceptibility to AS include ERAP-1... the IL-23 receptor and downstream signaling molecules... such as STAT3.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: How does the gut microbiota potentially trigger the inflammatory response in Ankylosing Spondylitis?
back: Microbial products penetrate the mucosal barrier, activating submucosal dendritic cells/macrophages to overproduce IL-23.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1094 (Book Page): [Fig 26.39] Gut flora/Microbial products [leads to] Activation of immune cells in gut submucosa [and] IL-23 [production].

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Which specific cytokine is implicated in driving new bone formation (syndesmophytes) in AS?
back: Interleukin-22 (IL-22). It is produced by T-cells and activates osteoblasts at inflammatory sites.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1094 (Book Page): [Fig 26.39] Production of IL-22 by T cells is thought to be involved in causing the new bone formation.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Explain the role of 'misfolding' in the pathogenesis related to HLA-B27.
back: HLA-B27 molecules may misfold, triggering endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, which leads to inflammatory cytokine release.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): HLA-B27 molecules may also misfold, causing increased endoplasmic reticulum stress. This could lead to inflammatory cytokine release by macrophages.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: What defines the transition from non-radiographic axSpA to Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS)?
back: The presence of structural damage on X-ray, such as definitive sacroiliitis or syndesmophyte formation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): A diagnosis of AS (radiographic axSpA), which requires evidence of these radiographic changes on X-ray, may only be applied many years after a patient’s symptoms started.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: What is the typical male-to-female ratio and prevalence of AS in most populations?
back:
Ratio: 3:1 (males:females).
Prevalence: Usually below 0.5%.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): For AS there is a male-to-female ratio of about 3:1. The overall prevalence of AS is below 0.5% in most populations.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: A 25M has inflammatory back pain and HLA-B27+ but normal X-rays. What is the most likely diagnosis?
back: Non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis (nr-axSpA). Diagnosis is supported by HLA-B27 and clinical features despite lack of X-ray changes.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [axSpA] includes... non-radiographic SpA (nr-axSpA) [and] radiographic axSpA (ankylosing spondylitis [AS])... radiographic alterations... are not present in patients with nr-axSpA.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Q: Which specific HLA allele is associated with more than 95% of Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) cases?
back: HLA-B27.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [There is a striking association with HLA-B27, particularly for AS (> 95%).]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Q: Describe the central cytokine axis driving the immunopathogenesis of axial spondyloarthritis.
back: The IL-23/IL-17 axis: IL-23 triggers Th17 lymphocytes to produce IL-17 and TNF-α, causing inflammation and bone remodeling.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [primarily mediated through increased production of IL-23, which in turn causes activation of Th17 lymphocytes that produce IL-17, TNF-α and other inflammatory cytokines.]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Q: What is the hallmark pathological musculoskeletal lesion in Ankylosing Spondylitis?
back: Enthesitis (inflammation at the site of ligament, tendon, or capsule insertion into bone).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [A hallmark lesion of SpAs is enthesitis, which is inflammation at the site of a ligament or tendon insertion into bone.]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Q: Name two non-HLA genetic variants that increase susceptibility to Ankylosing Spondylitis.
back: 1. ERAP-1 (antigen processing protein). 2. IL-23 receptor (IL-23R).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [Other susceptibility genes also implicated in susceptibility to AS include ERAP-1... the IL-23 receptor and downstream signalling molecules... such as STAT3.]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Q: Which cytokine is specifically implicated in causing new bone formation (syndesmophytes) in AS?
back: Interleukin-22 (IL-22), produced by T cells.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1094 (Book Page): [Production of IL-22 by T cells is thought to be involved in causing the new bone formation that occurs in of axial spondyloarthritis.]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Q: How is the gut microbiota hypothesized to trigger the immune response in AS patients?
back: Bacterial components (e.g., Klebsiella aerogenes) penetrate the mucosal barrier, activating submucosal macrophages and the IL-23/IL-17 axis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1094 (Book Page): [In genetically susceptible individuals, it is thought that bacterial components penetrate the mucosal barrier to activate macrophages and dendritic cells in the intestinal submucosa. These cells produce increased amounts of interleukin (IL)-23]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Q: List three hypothesized pathogenic mechanisms of the HLA-B27 molecule in AS.
back: 1. Abnormal antigen presentation. 2. Formation of HLA-B27 homodimers. 3. Misfolding leading to endoplasmic reticulum stress.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [The HLA-B27 molecule itself is implicated through its antigen-presenting function or because of its propensity to form homodimers... HLA-B27 molecules may also misfold, causing increased endoplasmic reticulum stress.]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Q: A 25-year-old male with chronic inflammatory back pain shows bone marrow oedema on MRI but a normal X-ray. Define the stage.
back: Non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis (nr-axSpA).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [Radiographic alterations, such as new bone formation with syndesmophytes and ankylosis, develop later in the course of the disease and, by definition, are not present in patients with nr-axSpA.]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Q: What is the morphological result of chronic calcification of the outer annulus fibrosus in AS?
back: Syndesmophytes (leading to the 'Bamboo Spine' appearance on X-ray).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1094 (Book Page): [Bridging syndesmophytes may also be seen. These are areas of calcification that follow the outermost fibres of the annulus... typical ‘bamboo’ spine]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Q: Why is IL-23 significant in the transition from gut inflammation to axial skeletal disease?
back: IL-23 produced in the gut activates Th17 cells, which then migrate to the axial skeleton to drive osteoclast activity and bone erosion.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1094 (Book Page): [These cells produce increased amounts of interleukin (IL)-23, which activate Th17 cells resulting in production of IL-17... driving inflammation, causing sacroiliitis and enthesitis.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What two primary factors drive the clinical manifestations and organ damage in systemic inflammatory vasculitis?
back: 1. Local tissue ischaemia (due to vessel inflammation/narrowing). 2. Systemic effects of widespread inflammation (fever, malaise, weight loss).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): [The clinical features result from a combination of local tissue ischaemia (due to vessel inflammation and narrowing) and the systemic effects of widespread inflammation.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: How does the pathological process of vessel wall necrosis contribute to multi-system complications in vasculitis?
back: Inflammation and necrosis lead to vessel wall destruction, which results in tissue infarction, organ damage (skin, kidney, lung, brain), and systemic inflammatory response.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): [Vasculitis is characterised by inﬂammation and necrosis of blood vessel walls, with associated damage to skin, kidney, lung, heart, brain and gastrointestinal tract.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Contrast the typical renal complications found in Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN) with those in Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA).
back: 1. PAN: Multiple renal infarctions and severe hypertension. 2. MPA: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Glomerulonephritis is notably rare in PAN.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1045 (Book Page): [Severe hypertension and/or renal impairment may occur due to multiple renal infarctions, but glomerulonephritis is rare (in contrast to MPA).]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: A patient with vasculitis develops saddle nose deformity and proptosis. What long-term destructive outcomes are suspected?
back: 1. Destruction of nasal bone and cartilage. 2. Retro-orbital inflammation (proptosis). 3. Vision loss from optic nerve compression (GPA features).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): [Untreated nasal disease ultimately leads to destruction of bone and cartilage... proptosis may occur because of inﬂammation of the retro-orbital tissue... loss of vision due to optic nerve compression.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Which pharmacological step is mandatory to prevent haemorrhagic cystitis during high-dose cyclophosphamide treatment for vasculitis?
back: 1. Aggressive hydration. 2. Co-prescription of Mesna (2-mercaptoethane sulfonate) to bind urotoxic metabolites.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1040 (Book Page): [Cyclophosphamide may cause haemorrhagic cystitis, but the risk can be minimised by good hydration and co-prescription of mesna (2-mercaptoethane sulfonate).]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Identify the funduscopic findings associated with catastrophic vision loss in Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA).
back: The optic disc appears pale and swollen with haemorrhages, resulting from occlusion of the posterior ciliary artery.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1046 (Book Page): [In such cases the optic disc may appear pale and swollen with haemorrhages, but these changes may take 24–36 hours to develop and the fundi may initially appear normal.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Why is screening for premature atherosclerosis essential in the long-term management of systemic vasculitis/SLE?
back: Chronic inflammation damages vascular endothelium. Risk is compounded by glucocorticoid therapy, smoking, and associated procoagulant antibodies.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1039 (Book Page): [The risk of cardiovascular disease is increased due to a combination of... effects of inﬂammatory cytokines on vascular endothelium, chronic glucocorticoid therapy and the effects of antiphospholipid antibodies.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: A patient with late-onset asthma develops asymmetric foot drop and purpura. Which neurological complication of vasculitis is this?
back: Asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex (a characteristic feature of the acute presentation of Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis [EGPA]).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1044 (Book Page): [The typical acute presentation is with a triad of skin lesions (purpura or nodules), asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex and eosinophilia.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Describe the physiological loop linking chronic inflammation to cardiovascular outcomes in systemic vasculitis.
back: Inflammatory cytokines -> Endothelial dysfunction -> Accelerated atherosclerosis -> Increased risk of stroke and myocardial infarction.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1039 (Book Page): [The risk of cardiovascular disease is increased due to a combination of conventional risk factors... effects of inﬂammatory cytokines on vascular endothelium, chronic glucocorticoid therapy...]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What is the most significant coronary complication of Kawasaki disease in pediatric patients?
back: Coronary artery aneurysms/arteritis, which can lead to myocardial infarction and peripheral vascular insufficiency.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1045 (Book Page): [Cardiovascular complications include coronary arteritis, leading to myocardial infarction, transient coronary dilatation, myocarditis, pericarditis, peripheral vascular insuf‑ciency and gangrene.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What are the characteristic long-term pulmonary outcomes seen on CT in patients with Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA)?
back:
- Migratory pulmonary infiltrates.
- Pulmonary nodules (often cavitating).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1104 (Book Page): Migratory pulmonary infiltrates and nodules occur in 50% of patients (as seen on high-resolution CT of lungs).

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Contrast the typical long-term renal outcomes between Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA) and Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN).
back:
- MPA: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
- PAN: Multiple renal infarctions and severe hypertension (glomerulonephritis is notably rare).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1105 (Book Page): Severe hypertension and/or renal impairment may occur due to multiple renal infarctions, but glomerulonephritis is rare (in contrast to MPA).

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Beyond nasal cartilage destruction, what orbital complication in GPA leads to permanent vision loss?
back:
- Proptosis caused by retro-orbital tissue inflammation.
- Mechanism: Direct compression of the optic nerve.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1104 (Book Page): proptosis may occur because of inflammation of the retro-orbital tissue... or loss of vision due to optic nerve compression.

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: A patient with refractory asthma develops mononeuritis multiplex. What is the likely diagnosis and its major long-term GI complication?
back:
- Diagnosis: Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA).
- GI Complication: Mesenteric vasculitis leading to abdominal pain or bowel infarction.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1104 (Book Page): asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex... Up to 50% of patients have abdominal symptoms provoked by mesenteric vasculitis.

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What are the mandatory long-term toxicities to monitor during Cyclophosphamide treatment for systemic vasculitis?
back:
- Hemorrhagic cystitis.
- Permanent infertility (azoospermia or premature menopause).
- Increased risk of bladder malignancy.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1100 (Book Page): Cyclophosphamide may cause haemorrhagic cystitis... because of the risk of azoospermia and premature menopause, sperm or oocyte collection and storage need to be considered.

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: List the hallmark vascular outcomes associated with long-term Takayasu Arteritis.
back:
- Vessel occlusion (causing claudication and bruits).
- Aortic coarctation.
- Aneurysmal dilatation and aortic incompetence.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1105 (Book Page): characterised by granulomatous inflammation of the vessel wall, leading to its occlusion... Aortic coarctation, and aneurysmal dilatation may also occur.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: What is the most significant genetic association with Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS), present in over 95% of cases?
back: HLA-B27 (Major Histocompatibility Complex class I molecule).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [There is a striking association with HLA-B27, particularly for AS (> 95%).]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Which specific immunological axis is the primary driver of mucosal and axial inflammation in AS pathogenesis?
back: The IL-23/IL-17 axis, mediated by the activation of Th17 lymphocytes.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [axSpA is thought to arise as the result of an aberrant host response to infection... primarily mediated through increased production of IL-23, which in turn causes activation of Th17 lymphocytes that produce IL-17.]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Identify the non-HLA gene that facilitates intracellular antigen processing and binding with HLA-B27 in AS.
back: ERAP-1 (Endoplasmic reticulum aminopeptidase 1).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [Other susceptibility genes also implicated in susceptibility to AS include ERAP-1 (an endoplasmic reticulum protein with a role facilitating intracellular antigen processing and binding with its presenting MHC molecule HLA-B27)]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: How does the 'misfolding' of the HLA-B27 molecule contribute to the pathogenesis of Ankylosing Spondylitis?
back: Misfolding induces endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, triggering inflammatory cytokine release by macrophages and dendritic cells.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [HLA-B27 molecules may also misfold, causing increased endoplasmic reticulum stress. This could lead to inflammatory cytokine release by macrophages and dendritic cells.]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Which specific cytokine is identified as the primary mediator of syndesmophyte (new bone) formation in AS?
back: Interleukin-22 (IL-22).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1094 (Book Page): [Production of IL-22 by T cells is thought to be involved in causing the new bone formation that occurs in axial spondyloarthropathy.]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Define the hallmark pathological lesion of AS occurring at the site of ligament or tendon insertion.
back: Enthesitis (inflammation at the enthesis).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [A hallmark lesion of SpAs is enthesitis, which is inflammation at the site of a ligament or tendon insertion into bone.]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Identify two intracellular signaling and receptor genes, besides HLA-B27, that predispose individuals to AS.
back:
1. IL-23 receptor (IL-23R)
2. STAT3 signaling molecules.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [Other susceptibility genes... include... the IL-23 receptor and downstream signaling molecules involved in directing Th17 cell responses, such as STAT3.]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: What role does the intestinal microbiota play in the immunopathogenesis of Ankylosing Spondylitis?
back: Microbial products penetrate the mucosal barrier, activating dendritic cells to produce IL-23 and trigger systemic Th17 responses.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1094 (Book Page): [In genetically susceptible individuals, it is thought that bacterial components penetrate the mucosal barrier to activate macrophages and dendritic cells in the intestinal submucosa. These cells produce increased amounts of interleukin (IL)-23.]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: A patient with HLA-B27 presents with back pain and syndesmophytes. Explain the role of IL-17 in this tissue damage.
back: IL-17 drives inflammation, leading to sacroiliitis, enthesitis, and bone erosion.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1094 (Book Page): [IL-17 has a pivotal role in driving inflammation, causing sacroiliitis and enthesitis... resulting in production of IL-17, tumour necrosis factor (TNF)-α and other inflammatory mediators.]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: What environmental pathogen is specifically associated with increased faecal carriage and exacerbations in AS patients?
back: Klebsiella aerogenes.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [Increased faecal carriage of Klebsiella aerogenes has been reported in patients with AS and may relate to exacerbation of both joint and eye disease.]

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Name three primary organ systems frequently damaged by local tissue ischaemia in systemic inflammatory vasculitis.
back:
1. Kidney (nephritis/failure)
2. Lung (haemorrhage/nodules)
3. Skin (necrosis/ulceration)
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1104 (Book Page): [Systemic vasculitis] associated damage to skin, kidney, lung, heart, brain and gastrointestinal tract.

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What dual mechanisms drive the clinical features and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis?
back:
1. Local tissue ischaemia (secondary to vessel narrowing/inflammation)
2. Systemic effects of widespread inflammation (cytokine release)
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1104 (Book Page): The clinical features result from a combination of local tissue ischaemia (due to vessel inflammation and narrowing) and the systemic effects of widespread inflammation.

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Contrast the typical long-term respiratory outcomes of GPA versus Eosinophilic GPA (EGPA).
back:
GPA: Nasal bone/cartilage destruction and pulmonary nodules.
EGPA: Severe, poorly controlled asthma and eosinophilia.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1104 (Book Page): [GPA] Untreated nasal disease ultimately leads to destruction of bone and cartilage... [EGPA] late-onset asthma that is often difficult to control.

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What pulmonary complication occurs in 30% of patients with antisynthetase (Jo-1) antibodies in inflammatory muscle disease?
back: Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1102 (Book Page): Interstitial lung disease occurs in up to 30% of patients and is associated with the presence of antisynthetase (Jo-1) antibodies.

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Which serious urological complication and preventive measure are associated with long-term cyclophosphamide use in vasculitis?
back:
Complication: Haemorrhagic cystitis.
Prevention: Good hydration and co-prescription of Mesna.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1104 (Book Page): Cyclophosphamide may cause haemorrhagic cystitis, but the risk can be minimised by good hydration and co-prescription of mesna.

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What is the primary long-term renal outcome associated with Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA)?
back: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (necrotising small-vessel vasculitis).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1104 (Book Page): Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) is a necrotising small-vessel vasculitis found with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: Why is the risk of premature cardiovascular disease significantly increased in systemic inflammatory vasculitis?
back: Combination of hypertension, chronic glucocorticoid therapy, and inflammatory cytokine effects on vascular endothelium.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1089 (Book Page): The risk of cardiovascular disease is increased due to... effects of inflammatory cytokines on vascular endothelium.

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: A patient with Behçet’s disease develops progressive paralysis. Which CNS region is most likely involved?
back: The Brainstem (causing pyramidal signs).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1106 (Book Page): Neurological involvement occurs in 5% and mainly involves the brainstem... causing pyramidal signs, cranial nerve lesions.

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: List the potential gastrointestinal outcomes of severe mesenteric vasculitis.
back:
1. Abdominal pain
2. Bowel infarction
3. Perforation
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1089 (Book Page): Mesenteric vasculitis is a serious complication, which can present with abdominal pain, bowel infarction or perforation.

category: Discuss potential complications and long-term outcomes of systemic inflammatory vasculitis
front: Q: What chronic inflammatory outcome in vasculitis/RA leads to nephrotic syndrome and renal failure?
back: Secondary Amyloidosis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1090 (Book Page): Amyloidosis is a rare complication of long-standing disease that usually presents with nephrotic syndrome.

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Q: What is the strongest genetic association for Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS)?
back: HLA-B27 allele, present in >95% of patients.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [There is a striking association with HLA-B27, particularly for AS (> 95%).]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Q: Which cytokine axis is central to the immunopathogenesis of axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA)?
back: The IL-23 / IL-17 axis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [abnormal mucosal immunity primarily mediated through increased production of IL-23, which in turn causes activation of Th17 lymphocytes that produce IL-17]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Q: Differentiate the pathological roles of IL-17 and IL-22 in Ankylosing Spondylitis.
back:
IL-17: Drives inflammation and sacroiliitis.
IL-22: Mediates new bone formation (syndesmophytes).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1094 (Book Page): [IL-17 has a pivotal role in driving inflammation, causing sacroiliitis and enthesitis. Production of IL-22 by T cells is thought to be involved in causing the new bone formation]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Q: A 24-year-old male with chronic inflammatory back pain tests positive for HLA-B27. What molecular mechanism links this allele to inflammation?
back: Possible mechanisms include antigen presentation, HLA-B27 homodimer formation activating leukocytes, or misfolding inducing ER stress and cytokine release.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [HLA-B27 molecule itself is implicated through its antigen-presenting function or because of its propensity to form homodimers that activate leukocytes. HLA-B27 molecules may also misfold, causing increased endoplasmic reticulum stress.]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Q: What non-HLA protein facilitates antigen processing for binding with HLA-B27 in AS susceptibility?
back: ERAP-1 (an endoplasmic reticulum protein).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [Other susceptibility genes also implicated... include ERAP-1 (an endoplasmic reticulum protein with a role facilitating intracellular antigen processing and binding with its presenting MHC molecule HLA-B27)]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Q: Define the hallmark pathological lesion characteristic of the spondyloarthritides.
back: Enthesitis: Inflammation at the site of ligament or tendon insertion into bone.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1093 (Book Page): [A hallmark lesion of SpAs is enthesitis, which is inflammation at the site of a ligament or tendon insertion into bone.]

category: Describe the genetic predisposition and immunopathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
front: Q: How is the intestinal microbiota conceptually linked to the development of axial spondyloarthritis?
back: Aberrant host response to gut flora triggers Th17 activation and production of IL-23, IL-17, and TNF-α.
